title: Inequality: A Tale of Two Stories
text:
Welcome
In 2013, Barack Obama called rising inequality “the defining challenge of our time.” Since then, the topic has moved from the margins of economics to the centre of public debate. Yet people who agree that inequality matters often mean very different things by it, read the same data in opposite ways, and propose opposite remedies.
This module takes that disagreement seriously. Its title, a tale of two stories, refers to the two narratives that dominate the debate: one of progress, in which global growth has lifted billions out of extreme poverty and countries have converged, and one of polarisation, in which societies drift apart and the gains of growth flow to the top. Both stories rest on empirical evidence. Learning to see which assumptions, measures, and theories of justice sit behind each story is the core skill this module trains.
The module accompanies the inequality session of the CDE Online International Bachelor and Master Winter School. It is an open educational resource by the Centre for Development and Environment (CDE), University of Bern, so anyone interested can use it. No prior knowledge of economics is required.

title: Inequality: A Tale of Two Stories
text:
Learning outcomes
After completing this module, you can:

distinguish key concepts of inequality (outcome and opportunity, vertical and horizontal, absolute and relative, individual and structural) and explain why the choice of concept is never neutral
explain how the Gini coefficient and the Palma ratio are constructed and name their limits
interpret the “elephant curve” in relative and absolute terms and explain why both stories about global inequality can be told with the same data
compare conventional explanations of rising inequality (technological change, globalisation) with structural explanations (weakening redistributive state, erosion of countervailing powers, financialisation)
evaluate policy options ranging from redistribution to pre-distribution and universal basic services, and position yourself in the debate

title: 1  Inequality: What’s in a Word?
text:
1.1 Why Should We Care About Inequality?
The word “inequality” is used loosely: sometimes it means poverty, sometimes unfairness, sometimes the gap between the rich and everyone else. But inequality always implies a comparison: between individuals, groups, regions, or countries, and with respect to something. This chapter sorts out the concepts, shows how inequality is measured, and asks how we can analyse where it comes from. It ends with the question that frames the whole module: which differences do we consider justified, and why?

title: 1  Inequality: What’s in a Word?
text:
NoteOpening question



Before reading on, finish this sentence with one word: “Inequality is …” Write down two or three answers. You will come back to them at the end of the chapter.



A sense of fairness
Start with a short clip from a famous experiment by primatologist Frans de Waal. Two capuchin monkeys exchange a stone for food. Both are content as long as both receive cucumber. Then one of them gets a grape for the same effort.

What had been acceptable a moment ago becomes unacceptable once a neighbour gets a better reward for the same work. A sense of fairness seems to run deep. (A note on the experiment: the monkeys live together in a social group and were only briefly separated into neighbouring cages for the test. Animal research nonetheless raises ethical questions, and noticing them is part of thinking critically about how knowledge is produced.)


A question of legitimacy
Inequality is not only a matter of feelings. Thomas Piketty opens Capital and Ideology with a claim about legitimacy:

“Every human society must justify its inequalities: unless reasons for them are found, the whole political and social structure stands in danger of collapse.” (Piketty 2020)

The idea is old. Plato argued that a state which wants to avoid civil disintegration must not allow extreme poverty or extreme wealth, and that the legislator should set acceptable limits to both. In The Laws, he proposes a fixed upper limit to how much property any citizen may own relative to the poorest. When disparities grow too large, they erode trust, weaken cooperation, and fuel social fragmentation.


A question for sustainability
Inequality is also an ecological question. How income and wealth are distributed shapes how societies consume, pollute, and use resources. Chancel (2022) shows that the global top 10% of emitters are responsible for almost half of all greenhouse gas emissions, while the bottom half of the world population causes about a tenth. The World Inequality Report 2026 adds a second perspective: if emissions are attributed to the owners of the companies and assets that cause them, the wealthiest 10% account for 77% of the emissions linked to private capital ownership, and the poorest half for only 3% (World Inequality Lab 2026).
This is also why reducing inequality within and among countries is one of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDG 10). Of all the goals, SDG 10 is perhaps the most political, because it touches on the question of who gets what, and who decides.






ImportantInequality and sustainability transformations



Inequality is both a cause and a consequence of the polycrisis: it drives overconsumption at the top, limits the capabilities of those at the bottom, and undermines the trust and cooperation that any transformation needs.

title: 1  Inequality: What’s in a Word?
text:
1.2 Equality of What?
In his Tanner Lecture of 1979, Amartya Sen asked a deceptively simple question: Equality of what? Before we can talk about fairness, we have to decide two things.








NoteWhere and among whom?




Within countries: between individuals, genders, ethnic groups, generations, or regions
Between countries: comparing average incomes of nations
Global inequality: among all people of the world, regardless of where they live











NoteOf what?



Income, wealth, health, education, opportunities, quality of life, voice and participation, exposure to climate risks, and more.




The choice of the focal variable (what we compare) and the reference unit (among whom) already shapes the answer. Income inequality in Switzerland, wealth inequality in Switzerland, and global income inequality tell three different stories.

Outcome or opportunity?
Much of the debate boils down to two perspectives:

Inequality of outcome occurs when individuals do not have the same level of material wealth or living conditions. It is usually measured in monetary terms.
Inequality of opportunity asks whether people have the same chances, regardless of circumstances they did not choose, such as their parents’ income, their gender, or where they were born.

Advocates of equality of opportunity often argue that as long as everyone has the same chances, nobody can complain about the results. But today’s outcomes are tomorrow’s opportunities: the income of your parents shapes your education, your health, and your network. A report by UNDP calls the opposition between the two a “false dichotomy”: outcome and opportunity are two sides of the same coin, and policies against inequality must address both (UNDP 2013).


The capability approach: from equality to equity
Sen’s capability approach shifts the focus from what people have to what they are able to do and to be.

Functionings are the beings and doings people value: being healthy, being educated, taking part in the life of the community.
Capabilities are the real freedoms to achieve these functionings.
Conversion factors (personal, social, and environmental) determine whether resources such as income or public services can be turned into functionings.


“A disabled person will likely find it harder to achieve important and worthwhile goals than will a nondisabled person, even assuming they have access to equivalent bundles of resources.” (Sen, cited in Robeyns 2005)

Two people with the same income may have very different real freedoms if one of them faces discrimination, has a disability, or lacks access to transport. Equalising income is therefore not enough. The capability approach moves us from equality (everyone receives the same input) to equity (what does each person need to reach a comparable level of well-being?). Martha Nussbaum extended the approach with a list of ten central capabilities that every society should secure for all its members, from bodily health to control over one’s environment.

title: 1  Inequality: What’s in a Word?
text:
1.3 Dimensions and Measures

Across dimensions and spaces
Two further distinctions help to sort out what a given number tells us.







Distinction
Meaning




Vertical inequality
Inequality among individuals or households, for example between the richest and poorest 10%


Horizontal inequality
Inequality among groups defined by identity, such as ethnicity, religion, gender, region, or age (Stewart 2005)


Absolute inequality
The size of the gap between groups, measured in money (for example, dollars)


Relative inequality
The proportional difference between groups, measured as ratios or shares



Vertical inequality tells us about the overall distribution. Horizontal inequality makes structural exclusion visible: it matters for social cohesion and conflict whether poverty is spread across society or concentrated in one ethnic group or region (Stewart 2005).
The absolute versus relative distinction will become central in chapter 2. A simple example shows why: a 10% increase on an income of 1,000 dollars is 100 dollars. A 10% increase on an income of 1,000,000 dollars is 100,000 dollars. In relative terms, both grew equally. In absolute terms, the gap widened by 99,900 dollars.


The Gini coefficient
The most widely used measure of inequality is the Gini coefficient. It is based on the Lorenz curve, which plots the cumulative share of the population (from poorest to richest) against their cumulative share of income. If everyone had the same income, the curve would follow the diagonal line of perfect equality.






Figure 1.1: Lorenz curves and inequality measures for two hypothetical societies. Own figure, illustrative data.



The Gini coefficient is the area between the line of perfect equality and the Lorenz curve (area A), divided by the whole area under the diagonal (A + B). It ranges from 0 (everyone has the same) to 1 (one person has everything).
The Gini is useful, but it has well-known limits (Hickel 2016; Trapeznikova 2019):

It is a relative measure. If all incomes grow by 10%, the Gini stays the same, even though the absolute gap between rich and poor grows.
It depends on what is measured. Values differ for wages, market income, disposable income (after taxes and transfers), consumption, and wealth. Wealth Ginis are typically much higher than income Ginis.
It is over-sensitive to the middle and captures changes at the very top and the very bottom poorly, because it is a calculation of an area.



The Palma ratio
The Palma ratio compares the income share of the richest 10% with that of the poorest 40%. It builds on the observation that the share of the middle classes (deciles 5 to 9) tends to be fairly stable across countries, so that most differences between countries come from the tails. In Figure 1.1, the richest 10% in society B earn 4.3 times as much as the poorest 40% together. The Palma is easy to communicate and responds to what happens at the top and bottom.






TipGood practice



No single number captures inequality. Complement the Gini with an absolute measure or the Palma ratio, and say clearly whether you measure income or wealth, before or after taxes, and within or between countries.

title: 1  Inequality: What’s in a Word?
text:
1.4 Individual or Structural?
How should we explain inequality? Two broad approaches compete.

Individual approach: inequality is analysed at the level of the individual. Economic inequalities are primarily the result of personal attributes and efforts: education, talent, choices, hard work. This is the dominant view in neoclassical (marginalist) economics.
Structural approach: inequalities are built into the structure of society and into social positions, for example through citizenship (where you are born) or your position in relation to the means of production (whether you own capital or sell your labour). This view is rooted in classical political economy and in post-Keynesian and Marxian traditions.

Think of a running race in which one runner starts on a clear track while three others have hurdles in their lanes. No matter how hard the three try, they tend to fall behind. The individual approach looks at the runners; the structural approach looks at the track.

From effort to structure
How much of your income is your own doing? Branko Milanovic, one of the leading researchers on global inequality, gives a striking answer:

“When you ask how much of the total income […] can be explained by the variable of the country of birth, you basically get an answer of 0.6. […] 60% of your lifetime income is determined by your place of birth.” (Milanovic, interview 2019)

Adding the income position of your parents, Milanovic estimates that about 80% of income differences across the world can be explained by two factors nobody chooses: country of birth (about 60%) and parents’ income (about 20%). The remaining 20% is left for effort, luck, and everything else. Milanovic calls the premium of being born in a rich country a “citizenship rent.” These numbers challenge the idea that inequality mainly reflects merit.


Position in relation to the means of production
Two hundred years ago, David Ricardo put distribution at the very centre of economics:

“The produce of the earth, all that is derived from its surface by the united application of labour, machinery, and capital, is divided among three classes of the community; namely, the proprietor of the land, the owner of the stock or capital necessary for its cultivation, and the labourers by whose industry it is cultivated. […] To determine the laws which regulate this distribution, is the principal problem in Political Economy.” (Ricardo 1817, Preface)

Landowners receive rent, capital owners profit, and workers wages. Who owns productive assets therefore shapes everything from income patterns to political power.
From the late 19th century, the marginalist revolution shifted the focus of economics from class-based distribution to individual utility and marginal productivity. In this view, each factor of production is paid according to what it adds to output: a worker who adds two cars a day is paid the value of those two cars. Distribution becomes a technical outcome of markets rather than a question of power.
Michał Kalecki (1954) brought distribution back into macroeconomics. In his model, “workers spend what they get and capitalists get what they spend.” Because workers spend most of their income, a higher wage share tends to raise demand. A higher profit share can boost investment, but only if profits are reinvested; otherwise it leads to weak demand and stagnation. Distribution is therefore not only a moral question but a question of macroeconomic stability.






NoteDeep dive: Inequality 101





The Institute for New Economic Thinking (INET) offers a short video series on the basics of inequality by Arjun Jayadev and Branko Milanovic: Inequality 101.

title: 1  Inequality: What’s in a Word?
text:
1.5 Beliefs and Theories of Justice
Different concepts and perspectives identify different causes of inequality, and therefore lead to different solutions. Which concepts we choose depends on our beliefs, our worldviews, our social backgrounds, and the theories of justice we hold. Even the measurement of inequality is not value-free. As Anthony Atkinson (1973) put it, conventional measures “embody quite arbitrary values about the distribution of income”; that no explicit judgement is needed to compute them “simply obscures” this fact.

Three families of theories of justice









Family
Core idea
View of inequality
Thinkers




Libertarian
Heavy weight on individual freedom and private property; the market is the best allocation mechanism
Not a problem as long as it results from free choices and voluntary exchange
Milton and Rose Friedman (Free to Choose, 1980), Robert Nozick (Anarchy, State, and Utopia, 1974)


Liberal egalitarian
Society is analysed in terms of its individual members; markets are efficient but produce poverty and inequality that the state can and should reduce
Acceptable only under fair conditions
John Rawls (A Theory of Justice, 1971), Ronald Dworkin


Collectivist
Society consists of social classes defined by their relation to the means of production
Structural, produced by the economic system itself
Marxian traditions, John Roemer; communitarian critiques such as Michael Sandel



Rawls invites us to imagine a veil of ignorance: if you did not know where in society you would be born, which rules would you choose? His difference principle allows inequalities only if they benefit the least advantaged. Sen criticised Rawls for focusing on resources (“primary goods”) and overlooking the diversity of people’s ability to convert them into a good life, which brings us back to the capability approach.
Utilitarianism (Jeremy Bentham, John Stuart Mill) offers yet another lens: the just action is the one that produces the greatest good for the greatest number. It has little to say about how that good is distributed.






NoteDeep dive: Michael Sandel’s Justice lectures





Michael Sandel’s Harvard course gives an accessible introduction to these theories. Start with Episode 1, “The moral side of murder”.





What do we believe?
Here is a thought experiment used in many classrooms. Divide the population of your country into five groups of equal size, from the poorest 20% to the richest 20%. Before looking at any data:

How do you think wealth is distributed among the five groups?
How should it ideally be distributed?

Then compare your answers with the data. For Switzerland, the richest 20% own the overwhelming majority of net wealth, while the poorest 20% own close to nothing or have net debts (SGB 2018). Studies consistently find that people underestimate how unequal their societies are, and that their ideal distribution is far more equal than both their estimate and reality. We return to this in section 4.5.


Conclusion

Accounting for inequality implies a debate about the level of difference that is ethically justifiable, politically negotiable, and economically viable. (Bader and Bieri 2017)







ImportantKey takeaways of chapter 1




Inequality always means a comparison: of something (income, wealth, capabilities) among someone (individuals, groups, countries).
Outcome and opportunity are two sides of the same coin.
Every measure makes value judgements. The Gini is relative and insensitive to the extremes; complement it.
Individual explanations focus on effort; structural explanations show that birthplace and parents’ income explain most income differences worldwide.
Our theories of justice shape what we see as a problem and which solutions we consider.

title: 2  A Tale of Two Stories
text:
2.1 Growth, Poverty, and Inequality
Now that we have sorted out what inequality means, we look at how it has evolved. This chapter focuses on income inequality and on the relationship between economic growth, poverty, and inequality. You will meet two stories about recent decades. Both are based on the same data. Your task is to work out what each story highlights, what it hides, and which one you find more convincing.

title: 2  A Tale of Two Stories
text:
We live by stories
In Sapiens, the historian Yuval Noah Harari argues that what distinguishes humans from other animals is our ability to believe in shared stories:

“You could never convince a monkey to give you a banana by promising him limitless bananas after death in monkey heaven.” (Harari 2014)

Because we believe in stories (nations, laws, money, markets), we can cooperate with countless strangers. The same holds for inequality. People accept hierarchies because they believe in collective narratives: meritocracy, national progress, market freedom. Which story about inequality do you believe in?


Is growth the solution or the problem?
Development strategies rest on assumptions about how three things are linked: economic growth, poverty, and inequality.

In one story, growth is the solution. A rising tide lifts all boats: growth reduces poverty, and inequality either falls over time or does not matter much as long as the poor are better off. This story underlies the trickle-down argument and is closest to the libertarian view of justice.
In the other story, growth as it is currently organised is part of the problem. Its gains are captured by those who already own assets, inequality rises, and poverty reduction stays far below what growth could deliver. This story is closer to liberal egalitarian and collectivist views.

The famous Kuznets curve (1955) proposed a middle ground: inequality first rises with industrialisation and then falls as economies mature. Later research has largely failed to confirm an automatic turning point. Where inequality fell, as in Europe and North America after 1945, this was driven by wars, crises, and deliberate policies such as progressive taxation and strong trade unions, not by growth as such (Piketty 2014; Scheidel 2017).
Since the 1980s, two stories coexist. One is of progress: hundreds of millions of people have left extreme poverty, largely thanks to growth in China, India, and Vietnam. The other is of polarisation: income and wealth have become concentrated at the very top, and many societies are drifting apart. The next two sections examine both.

title: 2  A Tale of Two Stories
text:
2.2 Story One: The Elephant Curve
One of the most famous graphs in inequality research shows how the incomes of people across the global income distribution grew between 1988 (just before the fall of the Berlin Wall) and 2008 (the global financial crisis). The horizontal axis ranks all people in the world from the poorest (left) to the richest (right). The vertical axis shows the growth of their real income, adjusted for purchasing power, over these 20 years.






Figure 2.1: Relative income growth by percentile of the global income distribution, 1988 to 2008. Graph: C. Bader, based on Lakner and Milanovic (2016) and World Bank (2016, p. 7).



Because of its shape, the graph became known as the elephant curve.






NoteBefore reading on



Look at the curve for one minute. Who gained most from globalisation between 1988 and 2008? Who gained least?


Two points stand out:

Point A, around the middle of the distribution, marks the largest relative gains, of 70 to 80%. These are mostly people in the emerging middle classes of Asia, above all in China.
Point B, around the 80th percentile, marks almost no gains. These are mostly lower middle classes in Western Europe and North America.

The very top of the distribution also gained strongly, and the very poorest gained relatively little.
The story this graph seems to tell is a story of progress and convergence: many of the poorer people of the world (on the left) gained more, in percentage terms, than most of the rich (on the right). Global inequality between countries has fallen, and extreme poverty has declined.
It also helps explain political tensions in rich countries: while hundreds of millions in Asia moved up, many in the lower middle classes of the Global North felt left behind. Populist backlashes and disillusionment with globalisation partly feed on this experience.

title: 2  A Tale of Two Stories
text:
2.3 Story Two: The Absolute View
Now look at the exact same data from a different angle. The red line shows not the percentage growth but the growth of income in dollars for each percentile.






Figure 2.2: Relative (black) and absolute (red) income growth by percentile of the global income distribution, 1988 to 2008. Graph: C. Bader, based on Lakner and Milanovic (2016) and World Bank (2016, p. 7). Values digitised from the original graph; approximate.



The picture changes dramatically. In absolute terms, the lowest 90% of the world population saw only small income gains, while the richest gained far more than anyone else. A large percentage increase on a very small income is still a small amount of money. Relative convergence can coexist with absolute divergence.
If global cooperation and growth produce gains, the question of how these gains are shared is unavoidable. From the absolute perspective, the story is not one of convergence, but of a world drifting apart.

Which poverty line?
The same tension appears in debates on poverty. In 2019, the anthropologist Jason Hickel published an article with the title “Bill Gates says poverty is decreasing. He couldn’t be more wrong.” The argument raises three questions you can ask of any poverty statistic:

The China effect. A large part of the global decline in extreme poverty happened in one country, China, under a development model far from the free-market recipe usually credited with it.
Which poverty line? The World Bank’s international extreme poverty line (USD 1.90 a day until 2022, USD 2.15 until 2025, now USD 3.00 in 2021 prices) is very low. The World Bank also publishes higher lines for lower and upper middle-income countries (USD 4.20 and USD 8.30 a day), and some researchers argue for lines of USD 10 or more to capture a decent life. With higher lines, the number of poor people has fallen much less, or has even risen.
Relative or absolute? Has the share of poor people fallen, or their number? Measured against what is needed to live a decent life where people live?



What do newer data say?
Gradín (2024) revisits global inequality trends from 1980 to 2020. He confirms that global inequality declined in relative terms since about 2000, mainly because of strong growth in China, India, and other emerging economies. In absolute terms, however, inequality kept rising.






ImportantKey takeaways of chapter 2 so far




In terms of dollar distances between people (absolute inequality), inequality has unequivocally increased, both between and within countries.
Global inequality in relative terms has declined since about 2000, mainly due to strong growth in China, India, and other emerging economies.
The exceptions are at the extremes of the distribution: stagnation among the very poor and rising concentration among the very rich.

2.4 Beyond Income: A Case Study and Your Own Graph

Case study: growth and poverty in Laos
Lao PDR is a good example of why the choice of measure matters. Between 2003 and 2013, the country recorded high economic growth and impressive poverty reduction: measured with the international monetary poverty line of USD 1.90 a day, poverty fell by about 40%.
But who benefited? A multidimensional analysis of poverty, which looks at deprivations in education, health, and living standards rather than income alone, tells a more mixed story (Bader et al. 2016, 2017):

Monetary and multidimensional poverty often do not identify the same people as poor. Policies targeting only the monetary poor miss many deprived households.
Over the same period, malnutrition remained widespread: according to the WHO, around 40% of children under five were stunted, a level of undernutrition that impairs development.
Inequalities within Laos are as large as global inequalities, and they follow horizontal lines: ethnic minorities in remote upland areas benefited far less from growth than the lowland majority.

Growth reduced income poverty, but it also increased disparities. A single monetary indicator hid both the persistence of non-income deprivation and the growing gaps between groups.

title: 3  Why Is Inequality Rising?
text:
3.1 The Conventional Wisdom
We have seen what inequality looks like. Now we ask why it has been rising in most countries since the 1980s. There is no single explanation: economists, sociologists, and political scientists offer different narratives. This chapter starts with the most common mainstream explanation and then moves to structural and political economy accounts. The central question is whether rising inequality is a natural market outcome or whether it is produced.
The standard explanation sounds neutral, almost technical. It rests on two forces.
Skill-biased technological change. Technological change transforms markets and the way we work. Automation and digitalisation increase the demand for highly educated workers. When education does not keep pace with technology, these workers become scarce, and the wage gap between them and less educated workers grows. More precisely, computers mainly replace routine tasks that follow clear rules, whether manual (assembly lines) or cognitive (bookkeeping, clerical work). Many of these were middle-income jobs. Non-routine work at the top (analysis, management) and at the bottom (cleaning, care, crafts) was much harder to automate. Economists therefore speak of routine-biased technological change and of a polarisation of the labour market (Autor et al. 2003; Goos et al. 2014).
Artificial intelligence may shift this pattern again. It is most capable in cognitive, office-based tasks such as writing, coding, and analysis, including well-paid ones (Eloundou et al. 2024). Crafts, care, and other work that relies on dexterity, physical presence, or human relationships is harder to replace. Such work is not less skilled, but differently skilled. Whether it will be better paid is an open question: wages depend not only on what machines can or cannot do, but also on who bargains for them and how society values different kinds of work. Care work, for example, has long been hard to automate and is still poorly paid. The evidence on AI and wages is still very recent.
Globalisation. Capital became mobile: firms can relocate production, outsource services, or automate. Labour remained largely national. Workers in rich countries were exposed to competition with workers in lower-wage countries, which put pressure on wages and labour standards.
In this story, inequality is the result of education gaps and global competition, not of power. The conclusion is that rising inequality is essentially a natural market process: you may not like it, but there is little you can or should do about it, except invest in skills and let the market adjust. The underlying assumption is that free markets pay workers according to their contribution.
Robert Reich, former US Secretary of Labor, argues that this conventional wisdom is not wrong, but that it leaves out some of the largest and most important changes. The next sections look at them.

title: 3  Why Is Inequality Rising?
text:
3.3 The Weakening Redistributive State
Many factors affect the distribution of income and wealth, and a large part of them are political. A first structural explanation concerns the state.
In OECD economies, taxes and transfers typically reduced the inequality of disposable income by one fifth to one quarter compared with market income (Dabla-Norris et al. 2015). In recent decades, this redistributive role has shrunk, for three reasons:

Reduced progressivity of personal income taxes: top marginal tax rates were cut sharply in most rich countries from the late 1970s onwards.
Lower taxes on capital and corporations, often justified as necessary for international competitiveness.
Tighter spending on social programmes due to austerity policies.

The effect is a redistribution upwards, concentrating income and wealth among those who own capital.

Rich countries, poor governments
The World Inequality Report 2022 shows a striking pattern: over the past 40 years, countries have become much richer, but their governments have become much poorer. In rich countries, the share of wealth held by public actors is close to zero or even negative, so that almost all wealth is in private hands. The COVID-19 crisis amplified this trend, as governments borrowed the equivalent of 10 to 20% of GDP, essentially from the private sector (Chancel et al. 2022). Poorer governments have less capacity to provide education, health, and security, and private companies increasingly take their place.


Commodification
There are two basic ways in which people get access to goods and services:

They are provided as a right of membership in a group, for example public health care or education for all citizens or residents.
They are purchased or otherwise secured by those with money.

Commodification is the process by which goods, services, and opportunities are increasingly allocated to those who can pay. The more essential things, such as housing, health, care, or education, are commodified, the more income inequality translates into inequality of capabilities. Rising commodification drives inequality and narrows the scope for state action.






ImportantThe core point



Inequality outcomes can be, and are, mediated by policies, rules, and legislation. Inequality is thus produced. To understand it, we need to analyse what has changed in these mediators.

section: 3.4 Countervailing Powers and the Use of Profits
text:
3.4 Countervailing Powers and the Use of Profits

Countervailing powers
In 1952, the economist John Kenneth Galbraith introduced the idea of countervailing powers: trade unions, cooperatives, small retailers, local banks, and public regulation that balance the power of large corporations. Capitalism, he argued, works in a socially acceptable way only when such counterweights exist. Since the 1980s, many of them have been weakened or dismantled: union membership has declined, labour markets were deregulated, and market concentration has grown.
Robert Reich (2020) describes the result as a vicious cycle: big money from large corporations, financial markets, and the wealthy shapes the rules of the economic and social game, and these rules in turn favour the top at the expense of everyone else. From this perspective, rising inequality is not only a market failure; it is also a policy success for those who benefit from it.


Productivity and wages
Mainstream theory says that wages reflect productivity: if workers produce more, they should earn more. For the decades after the Second World War, often called the “golden age of capitalism,” real wages in rich countries indeed tracked productivity.
Since then, a gap has opened. The International Labour Organization reports that in 52 high-income countries, labour productivity grew by 21.8% between 1999 and 2019, while real wages grew by only 14.3% (ILO 2020). The benefits of higher productivity are increasingly captured by the owners of capital rather than passed on to workers. Globally, the share of national income going to labour has declined (ILO 2019).






NoteHypothesis



The abolition of countervailing powers such as trade unions and the weakening redistributive role of the state have contributed to the gap between productivity growth and real wage growth in high-income countries.




Where do the profits go?
If productivity gains do not go to wages, where do they go? William Lazonick distinguishes two corporate strategies:







Retain and invest (value creation)
Downsize and distribute (value extraction)




Dominant from the 1940s to the 1970s
Dominant since the 1980s


Profits are reinvested: expanding skills, raising pay, hiring people, creating new products
Profits are paid out to shareholders through dividends and share buybacks; jobs become insecure and executive pay explodes

In a share buyback, a company purchases its own shares on the market. This reduces the number of shares, increases earnings per share, and typically lifts the share price, which benefits shareholders and executives paid in stock (Lazonick 2014). Some large companies have spent more than 100% of their profits on buybacks and dividends over several years, borrowing to pay out their shareholders. An analysis of Apple’s annual reports for 2012 to 2018 by the author of this module found such a pattern.
This links back to Kalecki (section 1.4): when profits rise but are not reinvested, demand weakens and growth slows. Financialisation, the growing weight of financial markets and motives in the economy, rewards existing wealth rather than productive activity and thereby amplifies inequality.

title: 3  Why Is Inequality Rising?
text:
3.5 How Wealth Concentrates: Synthesis
So far, we have mostly looked at income, a flow. Wealth is a stock: accumulated, often inherited, harder to see, and politically less contested. Wealth inequality is systematically larger than income inequality in every region of the world (Chancel et al. 2022). Why does wealth concentrate so persistently?

r > g
Thomas Piketty (2014) summarised one mechanism in a short formula: r > g. When the rate of return on capital (r) is higher than the growth rate of the economy (g), wealth grows faster than incomes from work, and those who already own capital pull ahead. Historically, r has exceeded g most of the time. The main exceptions were the decades after the two World Wars, when destruction, inflation, high taxes, and strong unions compressed inequality.
For Piketty, this is not a law of nature. Inequality, he argues in Capital and Ideology (2020), is ideological and political: markets, profits, wages, capital, debt, and tax havens are social constructs that depend on the legal, tax, and political systems a society chooses.


Matthew effects
Socio-economic research identifies cumulative advantage, or Matthew effects (“for whoever has, to him or her more will be given”): those with high incomes can save a larger share of their income than those with low incomes, and capital owners often earn higher returns than small savers. Both effects reinforce each other. Even pure chance can produce extreme concentration: if wealth grows by a random percentage each year, a small group ends up owning a large share over time, even without any systematic advantage. In such processes, the “average” outcome says little about what a typical person experiences.






NoteDeep dive: Thomas Piketty on Capital in the Twenty-First Century





Thomas Piketty: New thoughts on capital in the twenty-first century (Harvard Business Review video).





Synthesis
Based on the analytical lens of this module, rising inequality has several interacting causes:

Technological change has increased productivity, but not necessarily fair rewards.
Globalisation has shifted power from labour to capital.
Financialisation and asset inflation have enriched those who were already wealthy.
Institutional weakening has removed the counterweights that once protected workers and citizens.

Together, these forces have created a system in which inequality is self-reinforcing. And because it is produced by rules and institutions, it can also be changed.

title: 4  The Way Forward: Politics of Inequality
text:
4.1 Hardly the Silver Bullets: Growth and Education
We have analysed what inequality is, how it has developed, and why it is rising. Now comes the critical question: what can be done? If inequality is produced by rules and institutions, it can be reduced by changing them. Addressing inequality requires more than redistribution after the fact. It means rethinking how value is created, who owns productive assets, and how power is shared. This chapter presents five directions, building on the analytical lens of chapter 3, and ends by asking where you stand.
For decades, policymakers assumed that two things would fix inequality: economic growth and better education. Growth was seen as a tide that lifts all boats; education as the great equaliser.
Growth. As chapter 2 showed, growth can reduce income poverty. But growth is meaningless for reducing inequality if its gains keep going to the top 1% and little trickles down. In a world facing planetary boundaries, betting on ever more growth to solve distributional questions is also ecologically risky.
Education. Access to schools and better education has been, and will remain, an important lever towards more equal societies. But it does not do the trick alone. In The Tyranny of Merit (2020), Michael Sandel challenges the education argument. Based on the US, he describes a society built on the belief that “what you earn will depend on what you learn”:
This generates hubris among the winners and humiliation among the losers, and prepares the ground for authoritarian populism. Sandel also notes that stagnating wages despite rising productivity were not caused by workers’ lack of know-how, but by their lack of power (see section 3.4). Elizabeth Anderson makes a related point: productivity attaches mainly to work roles and to the capital put at a worker’s disposal, not to individuals. More education alone leads to credential inflation rather than to more equality.

4.2 Improve the Diagnosis
Policies can only be as good as the diagnosis they rest on. A first step is to substantiate the story of inequality with measures that are multidimensional, sensitive to the extremes, and inclusive of groups:

Poverty: multidimensional poverty measures look at deprivations in education, health, and living standards, not only income. As the Laos case showed (section 2.4), they often identify different people as poor than monetary measures do (Bader et al. 2016).
Inequality: the Palma ratio (section 1.3) and the Inequality-adjusted Human Development Index (IHDI) of UNDP, which discounts a country’s human development achievements by the inequality in their distribution.
Horizontal inequalities: data broken down by ethnicity, region, gender, or age make structural exclusion visible.
Wealth and the top: better data on wealth, inheritances, and top incomes, which household surveys tend to miss.

Such measures should be complemented by bottom-up, grounded experiences of what it means to be poor or excluded, and by tools to assess the distributional impact of a broad set of policies, including economic and fiscal policies. They build powerful arguments about inequality and how best to fight it.

section: 4.3 Beyond the Invisible Hand: Who Creates Value?
text:
4.3 Beyond the Invisible Hand: Who Creates Value?
Behind many debates on inequality lies a deeper belief: that the market is the best allocation mechanism, that market outcomes are objectively fair, and that the profits companies make are therefore entirely their own doing. From this belief follows that the state should not tax them much.
Mariana Mazzucato challenges this belief. In The Entrepreneurial State (2013) and Mission Economy (2021), she shows that many of the innovations underpinning modern economies, from the internet and GPS to the touchscreen and mRNA vaccines, would not exist without state-funded, high-risk research. The state does not only fix market failures; it actively creates and shapes markets. Yet the risks of innovation are often public, while the returns are private. The return on public investment, in this view, comes through taxes, public ownership stakes, or conditions attached to public funding.
This leads to three proposals:

Break up the myth that only business creates value. The economy is co-produced by public investment, private entrepreneurship, care work, and collective infrastructure. (Until the 1960s, banking and finance were not even counted as productive in national accounts; what counts as “value” is itself a political decision.)
Correct the fiscal bias in favour of capital. Today, labour is heavily taxed, and social security systems depend on it, which makes labour expensive. This creates incentives towards “excessive automation” that destroys jobs without necessarily increasing productivity (Brynjolfsson et al. 2020).
Redirect technological progress towards resource productivity rather than labour productivity: saving energy and materials rather than people.

title: 4  The Way Forward: Politics of Inequality
text:
4.4 From Redistribution to Fair Pre-distribution
Fiscal policy is not merely technical. It is a moral and political choice about what kind of society we want. Two complementary approaches exist.
Redistribution corrects market outcomes after the fact, through taxes and transfers:

higher taxes on capital, data, and resources relative to labour (Acosta 2017)
inheritance taxes, to counter the concentration of wealth and political power across generations (plutocracy)
international cooperation against tax avoidance: in 2021, more than 130 countries agreed on a global minimum tax of 15% for large multinational companies (OECD)

Pre-distribution aims to make the distribution of market incomes itself more equal, before taxes (Hacker 2011; Bozio et al. 2020). It acts on bargaining power, wage-setting rules, corporate law, and trade regimes:

limits on top pay, for example relative to the median wage in a company
living wages and job guarantees for the lowest-paid
broader ownership of capital, for example through employee stock ownership plans
democratising companies
universal basic services

Pre-distribution has gained support since the crises of recent years. After the 2007/08 financial crisis, governments argued they had no choice but to cut services. The COVID-19 pandemic showed that states do have other options: austerity was halted almost overnight and unprecedented fiscal resources were mobilised.

Re-embedding the economy
Karl Polanyi warned that when markets become “disembedded” from society, social and ecological crises follow. Two proposals aim to re-embed the economy.
Spreading ownership of capital. An employee stock ownership plan enables employees to own part or all of the company they work for. Yanis Varoufakis (2020) sketches a more radical version: every employee receives one share when hired, which cannot be sold, and which gives one vote. All major decisions are taken collectively, with the intranet acting as a permanent shareholders’ assembly. Equal ownership does not mean equal pay: employees decide together how revenues are split between costs, investment, basic pay, and bonuses. As Varoufakis asks, why should executives be paid in company shares, but not workers?
Universal basic services (UBS). Unlike a universal basic income, which pays cash, UBS focuses on collective provision of what everyone needs: housing, health care, education, care, mobility, and digital access (Coote and Percy 2020; Gough 2020). Its principles:

Services: collectively generated activities that serve the public interest
Basic: essential and sufficient to meet needs, not a minimal safety net for the “left behind”
Universal: everyone is entitled, regardless of their ability to pay

UBS counteracts commodification (section 3.3). It also links social and ecological goals: human needs, unlike wants, are limited and satiable, so meeting everyone’s needs within planetary boundaries is possible. Many services depend on people and relationships rather than on energy-intensive hardware. Examples range from public housing in Vienna to free public transport in Luxembourg and childcare in the Nordic countries.

title: 4  The Way Forward: Politics of Inequality
text:
4.5 Be Clear About Your Position

Where do incomes come from?
Your position in relation to the means of production (section 1.4) still matters. In rich countries, the median household receives most of its income, around 70 to 80%, from wages and salaries, and most of the rest from pensions and social security. For the top 0.01%, the picture is reversed: around 80% of their income comes from capital gains, interest, and dividends, and only about 15% from wages and salaries (SSRC n.d.).
Milanovic (2025) estimates that 77% of households in advanced and middle-income economies have zero or close to zero cash income from capital. If so few people own financial and productive capital, the gains from new technologies such as artificial intelligence, which raise the importance of capital, will accrue to those who already own it. Inequality would rise even if nobody became poorer.






NoteWhere are you?



Use the WID income comparator to see where you stand in the income distribution of your country and of the world.




Information revolution
Most people underestimate how unequal their societies are, and they tend to rank their own position higher than it actually is. Mijs (2021) finds a paradox: in more unequal societies, citizens are more likely to explain inequality in meritocratic terms, while people in more equal countries are more likely to see structural causes. Inequality and the belief in meritocracy go hand in hand.
Rising inequality does not seem to be a problem people constantly worry about. Awareness raising and better information could make it more tangible. If the structures and reward systems that reproduce inequality become visible, political preferences may shift and open the way for new initiatives in pre- and redistribution.






ImportantKey takeaways of chapter 4




Growth and education are important, but hardly silver bullets.
Better diagnosis comes first: multidimensional, group-sensitive measures and better data on wealth.
Value is co-created by the public and private sectors; tax systems should reflect this.
Pre-distribution (ownership, bargaining power, pay rules, universal basic services) complements redistribution.
Where you stand shapes what you see: be clear about your own position.
